extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in science studies, philosophers of science, and scientists interested in peer review and research-funding evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and community practices for reviewing scientific research proposals and publications, with emphasis on which criteria (e.g., Approach, Significance, Innovation) determine funding and publication outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding opportunity alignment / FOA specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must address the specific aims and constraints articulated in a Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) (example FOA: support studies to evaluate candidate cellular therapies to treat radiation-induced injuries in appropriate in vivo models when administered 24 hours or more post-irradiation, aimed toward FDA Animal Rule licensure pathway).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders deliberately shape which research variants are introduced by specifying narrow problems, models, timing, and regulatory/translation pathways; aligning a proposal closely with the FOA's explicit scope increases likelihood of being funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (proposal-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the standard review criteria: whether the proposed research addresses an important problem and its significance is typically judged by the strength, proximity, and number of connections to ongoing scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance is conceived relative to the community's established commitments; proposals that connect strongly to ongoing research or extend old, significant problems are favored. Funding agencies often distinguish scientific significance from broader societal impact (broader impact factors are divorced from core scientific significance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach (methodology/rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A core review criterion assessing the rigor, feasibility, and appropriateness of the research methodology; empirical data show differences in methodology esteem strongly predict overall proposal scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach is the most influential determinant of funding decisions (reported as almost twice as influential as Significance). It most directly measures epistemic properties and is weighted heavily; only expert peer reviewers tend to pay attention to Approach when forming overall assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation is an explicit review criterion but is treated cautiously: reviewers are warned to 'be cautious about seeming too innovative' since paradigm shifts may be resisted and novelty per se is not prized by practicing scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is valued at administrative levels but resisted in practice; novel approaches must demonstrate clear problem-solving virtues (e.g., computational ease, generality, ability to solve previously intractable problems) to be admitted. Appearing overly innovative can be penalized in review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators (PI qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess whether the principal investigators and project personnel are well qualified to conduct the proposed work (part of standard review criteria).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses suggest Investigator and Environment scores have relatively little influence on overall proposal assessment compared to Approach and Significance, though they remain standard checklist elements (assess experience, track record, team composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment (institutional/support context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the institutional setting and available resources will contribute to the project's success (standard review criterion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like Investigators, Environment tends to be a weaker predictor of overall assessment than Approach and Significance; nonetheless reviewers check for adequate facilities, institutional support, and fit with the proposed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication review: importance and sufficiency of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: In manuscript peer review, reviewers judge whether the research is important enough to warrant the community's attention and whether the evidence reported is sufficient to warrant the community's trust and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication review functions as a final community gate: importance (contribution to the field) and evidential sufficiency (quality/robustness of data and argument) are central. Adherence to a community's conceptual framework can affect these judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance judged via proximity to established problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A community tends to accept new problems as significant when they are either (1) old, established significant problems or (2) new problems closely related to old significant ones, using relatedness as a filter for potential significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This triage limits which new problems enter scientific practice; judges of significance focus on connections (strength, proximity, number) to ongoing research rather than external social priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of new problem-solving approaches: required virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: New methods/approaches are stringently resisted unless they show clear virtues over available approaches—virtues such as computational ease, generality, or success in dealing with previously insoluble problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel approaches must offer demonstrable problem-solving payoffs to overcome practitioner resistance. 'Novelty for its own sake is not a desideratum'—a new method must materially improve practice to be admitted into the community's toolkit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transmission and apprenticeship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of many research methods requires apprenticeship and multi-generational training; research publications cannot transmit the full expertise required to employ a method competently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because expertise is developed through apprenticeship, communities favor methodological continuity to ensure competent practitioners; adopting new methods entails long learning curves and may initially produce lower-quality outputs until several generations of practitioners adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between scientific significance and societal 'Broader Impacts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Major funding agencies (NIH, NSF, Research Councils UK) distinguish factors that make research significant for science from factors that make research significant for society (broader impact), and explicitly divorce these in review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing proposals, proposers should separate claims about scientific importance from broader societal benefits; reviewers typically evaluate these as distinct considerations and prioritize scientific (epistemic) criteria for core funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical weighting of review criteria (observed predictive magnitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative studies show most variance in proposal scores is explained by reviewers' esteem of the research methodology (Approach) and the research questions (Significance); Innovation is a weaker predictor (less than half as influential as Significance), and Investigators/Environment are relatively minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These empirical weightings imply that the more directly a criterion measures epistemic merits, the more influential it will be in reviewers' overall assessments. Emphasize methodological rigor and clarity of research questions in proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence and multiple discovery as indicators of epistemic selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-cultural convergence (e.g., adoption rates of techniques across countries) and multiple discovery (independent development of the same theory/technique) are cited as phenomena suggesting epistemic selection pressures rather than primarily social/contextual drivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent replication, widespread uptake across contexts, and multiple independent discoveries increase confidence that a research direction or method tracks epistemic merits; such patterns are used retrospectively to argue for epistemic efficacy of selection mechanisms.
